text:
The ink was faded, a bruised purple against the yellowed cardstock. It wasn’t just old; it was ancient, preserved in the dry air of the attic like a pressed flower. The handwriting belonged to Elara, my great-grandmother, who had passed away forty years before I was born. Yet, here was her script, looping and elegant, describing a lemon drizzle cake that no one in our family had ever tasted.

I traced the letters with a trembling finger. *Zest two lemons,* she wrote. *Whisk until the arms ache.* There was a strange intimacy in the instruction, a ghostly hand guiding mine across decades. The recipe didn’t list measurements in cups or grams, but in feelings: *a handful of hope, a pinch of sorrow.* It felt less like cooking instructions and more like a confession.

As I gathered the ingredients, the kitchen filled with the sharp scent of citrus. When I finally bit into the warm slice, the flavor was impossible—bright, bitter, and sweet all at once. It tasted like memory itself. For a fleeting second, the silence of the house broke, replaced by the phantom sound of laughter from another century. I wasn’t just eating a cake; I was consuming time, digesting the life of a woman I never knew, yet suddenly understood.
